claims.text: An MLIP workflow with on-the-fly free-energy reweighting can compute high-temperature fusion and phase free energies.
The proposed workflow will cost substantially less than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD.
The proposed workflow can retain fidelity comparable to explicit ab initio methods in both solid and liquid phases.
A limited ab initio training set can capture vibrational spectra, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling in both solid and fluid states.
Thermodynamic integration or free-energy perturbation can correct the MLIP so that phase free energies and relevant entropy terms are accurately reproduced.
Near melting, both solid and liquid free energies, including vibrational and anharmonic contributions, are essential.
The method is typically validated on elemental or binary systems before extension to multicomponent systems.
Similarity of bonding characteristics enables extension from elemental or binary systems to high-entropy alloys.
Accurate reproduction of vibrational entropy, anharmonic lattice effects, and electron–vibration coupling mediates reliable free-energy predictions.
Replacing explicit ab initio molecular dynamics with MLIP simulation greatly accelerates configurational sampling while retaining detailed atomic interactions.
Reweighting against a limited amount of accurate ab initio free-energy data corrects systematic MLIP biases across phase boundaries.
The method should reproduce phase free energies, melting temperature, and entropy contributions with accuracy comparable to explicit ab initio methods.
The method should reduce computational cost by approximately one to two orders of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD and full ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluations and TOR-TILD are accurate but computationally expensive.
The computational expense of the baseline methods is especially severe for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The approach is expected to work reliably for elemental and binary systems near fusion.
The approach can extend to multicomponent alloys if the training set spans their diverse local chemical environments.
New bonding environments in complex alloys may require additional validation and training data.
It remains unproven that limited ab initio reweighting data can fully correct MLIP deficiencies in subtle phase free-energy and entropy differences.
